_README: The whole editing surface for catechumens.html. `npm run faq` renders it into the blocks marked <!-- BUILD:name --> … <!-- /BUILD:name --> on that page and touches nothing else. Add a question by adding an entry here — never by writing a card into the markup, which is how the same answer ends up on the page twice in two wordings. The page's headings and prose are hand-written source; only the question cards come from this file.
_rules: An answer here is either something the parish has approved or something already published on another page of this site, and `source` records which. Nothing else may be written into `a`.

A question whose answer depends on this parish's pastoral practice is left `pending: true` until Fr. John supplies the wording. The card then says so on its face. That is the point of the page, not a gap in it — see QUESTIONS-FOR-FR-JOHN.md, which is generated from this file.
`askFather: true` adds the line routing the reader to Fr. John. Use it wherever the general answer cannot settle an individual's case, INCLUDING on questions that already carry an answer.
`verify: true` emits a <!-- TODO: verify --> marker, exactly as the calendar renderer does. Use it for a claim nobody has sourced yet.
`reviewed` is the date the wording was last checked against its source. Null while pending.

questions.q: What is an inquirer?
questions.preview: Someone who is asking questions about the Orthodox Church. Nothing is being asked of you in return.
a: An inquirer is simply someone who is looking into the Orthodox faith — coming to services, reading, asking questions, and seeing what the life of the Church is like from the inside.
No commitment is implied. Inquirers' conversations happen quietly and at your own pace, often over many months. You are welcome to keep coming, keep reading, and take as long as you need.
questions.source: faith.html, ntgocFaithTopics — parish-approved wording already published on this site
questions.keywords: inquirer enquirer visiting new asking questions start beginning

questions.q: What is a catechumen?
questions.preview: Someone the Church has formally set on the path towards being received, and who is being taught along the way.
a: A catechumen is someone who has moved from looking on to preparing: the Church has received them as a learner, prays for them by name in her services, and teaches them in the time before their baptism or chrismation. The word is as old as the Church herself.
How a person becomes a catechumen here, and what that time looks like at the Nativity, is Fr. John's to describe rather than ours.

link.label: How people become Orthodox, on our parish site

questions.q: Do I need to be sure I want to become Orthodox before I start asking questions?
questions.preview: No. Questions come first, and they are welcome long before any decision is.
a: Speak with Fr. John — no commitment is implied by it. People ask questions here for a long time before anything is decided, and some never move beyond asking. Both are honourable.
You are welcome to keep coming, keep reading, and take as long as you need.

questions.q: Why do Orthodox Christians have patron saints?
questions.preview: Because the saints are alive in Christ, and we ask for their prayers as we would ask a friend's.
a: Orthodox Christians honour the saints and ask for their prayers. A patron saint is one of them given to you by name: someone whose life you come to know, whose feast becomes your own day, and whose prayers you ask for as long as you live.
A Cloud of Witnesses, a free resource made by members of this parish, is a good place to begin reading about them.

questions.q: How do I choose one?
questions.preview: Read about the saints, pray, and talk it over with Fr. John. There is a quiz that will give you somewhere to start.
a: Most people arrive at a saint by reading, by praying, and by talking it over with their priest and their godparent — often a saint whose life rhymes with their own, or whose feast already falls near a day that matters to them.

A Cloud of Witnesses has a patron saint quiz, which is a gentle way in if you do not know where to start. Treat it as a way of meeting saints you had not heard of, not as an answer: the choice is made with Fr. John.

questions.q: What is a name day?
questions.preview: The feast of your patron saint — the day the Church keeps their memory, and with it, yours.
a: Your name day is the feast of the saint whose name you bear. Among Orthodox Christians it is greeted much as a birthday is, and often more warmly: “Many years!” is the thing to say.
The Church's calendar of the saints, day by day, is on A Cloud of Witnesses.

questions.q: Can I receive Holy Communion?
questions.preview: Not yet. Holy Communion is received by Orthodox Christians who are properly prepared — which is what you are preparing for.
a: Holy Communion is received by Orthodox Christians who are properly prepared to receive the Eucharist. Until you are received into the Church, you do not come to the chalice — and that is not a judgement on you, it is the thing the whole catechumenate is pointed towards.
When your first Communion will be is part of your reception, and Fr. John will tell you.

questions.q: Can I receive antidoron?
questions.preview: Yes. Antidoron is blessed bread that anyone present may receive, including those who are not Orthodox.
a: Antidoron is blessed bread that anyone may receive, including visitors who are not Orthodox. It is normally given by the priest after the Divine Liturgy concludes, as people leave for the hall — so you will pass him on your way out, and you are welcome to take a piece.
It is not Holy Communion. It is bread that has been blessed, given as a sign of the shared life of the parish.

questions.q: Can I light candles?
questions.preview: Yes. A candle is a small offering made with a prayer, and you are welcome to light one.
a: A candle is a small offering made with a prayer — for someone you love, for someone who has died, or for yourself. The flame is also an image: Christ is the Light of the world, and a lit candle is one of the Church's oldest ways of saying so.
You are welcome to light one when you come. You are equally welcome not to.

link.label: More of what you saw on Sunday

questions.q: Can I venerate icons?
questions.preview: Yes. Venerating an icon is something like kissing a photograph of someone you love.
a: Orthodox Christians venerate icons; we do not worship them. Worship belongs to God alone, and the honour given to an icon passes to the person shown in it, not to the wood and paint.
Nobody is watching to see whether you do it, or checking that you do it correctly. Follow the person in front of you, or simply stand and pray.

questions.q: Can I make the sign of the Cross?
questions.preview: Yes — it is prayer made with the body, not a gesture that has to be got right.
a: The thumb and first two fingers are joined to confess the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit — three, and one. The remaining two fingers are folded to the palm, confessing that Christ is both God and man.
It is prayer made with the body, not a gesture that has to be got right, and nobody is expected to join in before they are ready.

questions.q: Can I participate in parish life before I am Orthodox?
questions.preview: In most of it, yes. Come to the services, stay for coffee hour, and get to know people.
a: Most of the life of the parish is open to you now: the services, coffee hour, the festival, the classes and the ordinary work of keeping a church going. Coming to those things is a good deal of what the catechumenate is.
The sacraments are the part that waits, and a few roles are for Orthodox Christians. Where a particular thing sits, ask Fr. John.

questions.q: Can I attend coffee hour?
questions.preview: Yes, and please do. It is where most people actually meet the parish.
a: Our Sunday doesn't end when the service does. After the Divine Liturgy we gather in the parish hall for coffee hour — a shared, potluck-style meal, and an old Christian habit of sitting down to eat together after worship.
You do not need to know anyone to come in, and you do not need to explain yourself at the door.

questions.q: When are services?
questions.preview: Every Sunday: Orthros at 9:00 a.m., Divine Liturgy at 10:00 a.m. Weekday and feast-day services are on the calendar.
a: Sunday morning is Orthros at 9:00 a.m., followed by the Divine Liturgy at 10:00 a.m. They are two distinct services; people arrive across both.
Feasts, Paraklesis and the services of Holy Week are kept as they fall, so the parish calendar is the place to check.

questions.keywords: services times when sunday schedule orthros liturgy

questions.q: What is Orthros?
questions.preview: The morning service that comes before the Divine Liturgy. Here it begins at 9:00 a.m.
a: Orthros is the Church's morning prayer — psalms, hymns for the day, and the Gospel of the Resurrection on a Sunday. It leads straight into the Divine Liturgy without a break, which is why the two can sound like one long service.
You are not late if you arrive during it, and you are not late if you arrive after it either.
questions.source: General Church usage; the 9:00 a.m. start is data/site.json → serviceTimes
questions.keywords: orthros matins morning service before liturgy

questions.q: What is the Divine Liturgy?
questions.preview: The Sunday service of the Church, at whose heart is Holy Communion. Here it begins at 10:00 a.m.
a: The Divine Liturgy is the central service of the Orthodox Church: scripture, prayer and hymns leading to the offering of the Eucharist. Most Sundays here it is the Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom.
Services are approximately 50% Greek and 50% English, and congregational portions — the Creed, the Lord's Prayer — are offered in more than one language.

link.label: The Divine Liturgy, on our parish site

questions.q: Where should I sit?
questions.preview: Anywhere. There is no reserved seating.
a: There is no reserved seating. Sit where you like — towards the back is easy if you would rather watch before joining in, and nobody will move you on.
People come and go a little during Orthros, and stand and sit at different moments. Follow along if you want to; sit when you need to.

questions.q: How do I follow the service book?
questions.preview: Take a Greek-English Divine Liturgy book from a greeter or from the pew. It stays in the church.
a: A Greek-English Divine Liturgy book is available from a greeter or in the pew, with the service in both languages side by side. It stays in the church at the end of the service.
Following it is easier than it looks, and losing your place is normal. Much of the Liturgy repeats week to week, and you will know it sooner than you expect.

questions.q: What does “Kyrie eleison” mean?
questions.preview: “Lord, have mercy.”
a: Kyrie eleison — “Lord, have mercy.” You will hear this response again and again throughout Orthodox worship.
Even if you know no other Greek, it probably won't be long before you recognise it.
